sentences.text: Ohmdenosaurus was a sauropod dinosaur belonging to the class Saurischia that lived in what is now Germany during the Early Jurassic epoch.
This primitive sauropod was an obligate quadruped with a relatively short neck and a robust body.
Rupert Wild originally estimated the total body length at 3 to 4 meters, though a later re-evaluation suggests a length of 6.7 meters and a weight of 1.3 tonnes.
It is the only dinosaur identified from the Posidonia Shale.
Wear marks on the disarticulated bones suggest the animal died on land before its remains were washed into the sea and buried.
The only known specimen consists of a tibia and ankle bones found in the Posidonienschiefer in Baden-Württemberg, Germany, in 1978.
Its fossils were originally described as plesiosaur remains until a 1978 review of the holotype identified them as sauropod fossils.
German paleontologist Rupert Wild identified the remains as a sauropod in the 1970s and formally described the fossil as a new genus and species, Ohmdenosaurus liasicus, in 1978.
The name Ohmdenosaurus is derived from the village of Ohmden and the Greek word for lizard.
Ohmdenosaurus was a terrestrial animal whose fossil was transported at least 100 km from the shoreline before burial.
The tibia preserves muscle attachment sites, including a cnemial crest projecting about 4 cm and a crista lateralis running about 13 cm.
The medial condyle of the tibia is significantly larger than the broken lateral condyle and sits 2 to 3 cm lower.
The calcaneus is circular, measuring 43 mm in diameter and 15 mm in height.

Rupert Wild identified several small elements between 5 and 30 mm in size below the tibia's lateral condyle as cartilage, arguing they may represent sesamoids due to the high stress experienced in that area.
It is debated whether the small elements near the ankle are sesamoids or calcified pieces of the astragalus cartilage.
One study concluded that Ohmdenosaurus was a eusauropod.
The non-convex shape of the astragalus suggests Ohmdenosaurus was a very basal sauropod.
Recent discoveries suggest Ohmdenosaurus may be less basal than previously thought and more closely related to gravisaurs.
The genus and species authorities are both attributed to Wild, 1978.
Ohmdenosaurus lived during the early Toarcian age, approximately 182 million years ago.
The fossil dates to the early Toarcian, approximately 182.0 to 175.6 million years ago.
It lived on a series of islands in what is now the Bohemia region, where the nearest landmass was probably the Black Forest Massif about 100 km to the southwest.
